802.1X: IEEE standard for port-based network access control
A device must authenticate before the switch port or wireless association is allowed
Three roles: supplicant (device), authenticator (switch or access point), authentication server (usually RADIUS)
Uses EAP methods such as EAP-TLS and PEAP
Used for Wi-Fi Enterprise and wired NAC; failed devices are denied or put in a quarantine VLAN
Access badge: Physical card or token that identifies its holder and is presented to a reader to unlock doors
Often uses an RFID chip or magnetic stripe
Tailgating risk: someone follows a badged employee through a door
Weak RFID badges can be cloned
Often paired with access control vestibules
Access control vestibule: Small enclosed space with two interlocking doors between an unsecured and a secured area
Lets only one verified person through at a time; the second door unlocks after the first closes
Primary physical control against tailgating and piggybacking
Account lockout: Automatically disables an account after a set number of consecutive failed logins
Mitigates brute force and password guessing
Policy sets a threshold (for example five attempts) and a duration, or requires an admin unlock
Trade-off with availability: legitimate users can lock themselves out, which attackers can abuse as a denial of service
Account provisioning and deprovisioning: Provisioning creates accounts and assigns access by role when someone joins or changes jobs
Deprovisioning removes or disables access promptly when they leave or no longer need it
Identity systems and automation keep it consistent
Supports least privilege; orphaned or lingering accounts are a classic risk
Accountability: Ability to trace actions back to the specific user, system or process responsible
Holds users responsible for their actions after the fact
Active reconnaissance: Gathering information by directly interacting with the target
Examples: port scans, ping sweeps, banner grabbing, vulnerability scans
Can be detected by the target's security tools
Contrast passive reconnaissance, which never touches the target
Adaptive identity: Access rights are re-evaluated continuously from real-time context
Context includes location, device health, time of day and behavior patterns
Identity-based risk scoring changes during a session, not just once at login
Advanced persistent threat: Sophisticated, well-resourced attacker, often nation-state sponsored
Gains access and stays undetected for a long time
Pursues long-term goals such as espionage or data theft, not quick financial gain
Marked by stealth, patience and significant funding
Adware: Software that displays or downloads unwanted ads
Can track browsing behavior and slow the system
Sometimes opens the door to more serious malware
Air-gapped network: Network or system physically isolated from all other networks, including the internet
The strongest form of network isolation, used for industrial control systems or classified environments
Still needs physical and removable-media controls, because data can cross the gap on USB drives
Alert tuning: Adjusting detection rules, thresholds and exceptions so alerts reflect real threats
Cuts false positives and alert fatigue without missing genuine incidents
Baselines and business context improve it
Compare false positives and false negatives
Allow list and deny list: Allow list (whitelist): permits only explicitly approved items and blocks everything else
Deny list (blocklist): blocks specific known-bad items and allows everything else
Allow lists follow default deny: stronger, but need more upkeep
Deny lists are easier to run but miss unknown threats
Changes to either list are a technical implication in change management
Amplification attack: DDoS technique: small requests with a spoofed source address (the victim's) sent to servers
Servers such as open DNS, NTP or memcached reply with much larger responses to the victim
Reflection hides the attacker; amplification multiplies the volume
Defenses: close open resolvers, rate limiting, ingress filtering (BCP 38), scrubbing services, RTBH
Application allow list: Lets only approved applications run and blocks everything else by default
Stops malware and unapproved software even when no signature exists
Tools include AppLocker and Windows Defender Application Control
A default-deny model that needs maintenance when software changes; also called application whitelisting
ARP poisoning: Sends forged ARP replies so devices map the attacker's MAC address to a legitimate IP, often the default gateway
Lets the attacker intercept or alter traffic on the local network
A common way to get an on-path position on a LAN
Defenses: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI), static ARP entries, port security, segmentation
Asset management: Tracking hardware, software and data assets throughout their lifecycle
Each asset has an owner, a classification and security controls
Lifecycle: acquisition and procurement, assignment and accounting, monitoring and tracking, disposal or decommissioning
Disposal involves sanitization, destruction, certification and data retention
Asymmetric encryption: Uses a mathematically linked key pair: a public key shared openly and a private key kept secret
Data encrypted with one key can only be decrypted with the other
Solves the key-distribution problem of symmetric encryption, usually at the cost of speed
Encrypt to someone with their public key; sign with your own private key
Attack surface: Sum of all points where an unauthorized user could try to enter or extract data
Includes software, hardware, network and human factors
Reduce it by hardening and by disabling unused services and ports
Attack vector: Specific path or method a threat actor uses to gain unauthorized access
Examples: email, removable media, web application, wireless, supply chain, social media
Scenarios ask you to identify which vector is being described
Attestation: Formally verifying and vouching for the integrity, configuration or compliance of a system or claim
Often produces a signed statement a relying party can check
Remote attestation: a device cryptographically proves its firmware or boot state is untampered
Can also mean a vendor formally vouching for compliance with a standard
Attribute-based access control: Decides access by evaluating attributes of the subject, the object and the environment against policy rules
Examples: job title, data sensitivity, device health, time of day, location
RBAC, by contrast, relies on a single assigned role
Authentication: Verifying that an entity, such as a user, device or system, is who or what it claims to be
Proves identity; authorization is what grants access
Authentication token: Hardware or software item that generates or stores a credential used to prove identity
Examples: a key fob with a rotating code, an authenticator app (TOTP), an API or session token
A hard token is a physical device; a soft token is an app
A something-you-have factor; in OAuth, token also means an access or session token, so read the context
Authorization: Granting or denying an authenticated entity specific permissions to resources, based on policy
Authenticated but still denied access is an authorization failure
Automation and orchestration: Automation uses scripts and tools to do individual tasks without manual effort
Orchestration coordinates many automated tasks and systems into end-to-end workflows
SOAR platforms do this in security operations
Benefits: efficiency, enforcing baselines, secure scaling, faster reaction, workforce multiplier
Drawbacks: complexity, cost, single point of failure, technical debt, supportability
Availability: Authorized users have reliable, timely access to information and systems when needed
Protected by redundancy and fault tolerance
The A in the CIA triad
Backdoor: Hidden way to bypass normal authentication or security controls
Installed by malware or a malicious insider, or left by developers for testing and forgotten
A common payload of a trojan
Backout plan: Predefined steps to reverse a change and return to the previous working state if it fails
Normally required before a change is approved
Part of change management, with approvals, impact analysis, testing and a maintenance window
Also called a rollback plan; a change without one is a red flag for the change advisory board
Backup: Copy of data or systems stored separately so it can be restored after loss, corruption, deletion or disaster
Measured by how often it runs (RPO), where it is stored and how long a restore takes (RTO)
Types: full, incremental, differential, snapshot; onsite versus offsite
Keep one copy offline or immutable so ransomware cannot reach it
Baseline configuration: Documented, approved standard set of security settings and software configurations for a system type
A reference point for detecting unauthorized changes and keeping deployments consistent
Compare against the current state to spot configuration drift
Deviation from baseline can signal unauthorized change or compromise
Biometrics: Authentication factor based on something you are
Uses unique physical or behavioral traits: fingerprint, facial geometry, iris, voice
FAR: impostors wrongly accepted; FRR: legitimate users wrongly rejected
CER (crossover error rate) is where FAR and FRR are equal, used to judge accuracy
Birthday attack: Collision attack based on the birthday paradox of probability
Finding two inputs with the same hash needs far fewer attempts than brute-forcing one specific hash
Explains why collision attacks beat brute-force intuition
Defense: hash digests with enough output length
Bloatware: Unwanted software pre-installed by the manufacturer or bundled with other programs
Wastes resources and may contain vulnerabilities or telemetry
Removed during hardening; related to PUPs and adware
Block cipher: Symmetric algorithm that encrypts data in fixed-size chunks
Often needs padding and an operation mode, such as CBC or GCM, for data that does not fit evenly
Stream ciphers instead process data continuously, bit by bit
Blockchain: Transactions are grouped into cryptographically linked blocks
Validated by decentralized consensus, with no central authority
Gives integrity and non-repudiation for a shared history, not confidentiality
Blue team: Internal or hired group of defenders who monitor, detect and respond to threats
Uses SIEM, IDS/IPS and monitoring tools
Responds to attacks simulated by a red team during an exercise
Compare red, purple and white teams
Bluejacking: Sending unsolicited messages or contact cards to nearby Bluetooth devices
More of an annoyance: it does not steal data
Mitigation: set Bluetooth to non-discoverable or turn it off when not in use
Bluesnarfing: Unauthorized access to a Bluetooth device to steal data
Targets contacts, calendar entries and messages
Exploits vulnerable pairing or protocol flaws
Defenses: turn off Bluetooth, disable discoverable mode, patch firmware, require pairing approval
Bollard: Short, sturdy vertical post, usually in a row, set in the ground
Blocks vehicles from a pedestrian area or building entrance while people can walk through
Fencing, by contrast, blocks both people and vehicles along a perimeter
Botnet: Network of compromised, internet-connected devices (bots) controlled remotely by an attacker
Used for DDoS, spam and large-scale cryptomining
Brand impersonation: Attacker mimics a well-known company's logos, branding, email templates or look and feel
Deceives victims into trusting a fraudulent message, website or call
A broad deception tactic that can combine with phishing, typosquatting or vishing
Relies on borrowed visual or verbal trust, not a single technical method
Broadcast domain: Group of devices that receive each other's broadcast frames: all devices on the same Layer 2 network
Switches forward broadcasts to every port in a VLAN; routers do not forward them
Each VLAN and each router interface is its own broadcast domain
Smaller domains mean less noise and a smaller area for broadcast-based attacks like ARP poisoning and rogue DHCP
Brute force attack: Systematically tries every possible combination of characters or keys until the correct one is found
Needs lots of computation but eventually succeeds given an unlimited attempt budget
Differs from a dictionary attack, which tries a curated wordlist
Mitigations: account lockout, key stretching, strong long passwords
Buffer overflow: Program writes more data to a memory buffer than it was allocated to hold
Can overwrite adjacent memory and allow code execution
Mitigations: input validation, bounds checking, secure coding, DEP and ASLR
Bug bounty program: Rewards independent researchers with money or recognition for responsibly reporting valid vulnerabilities
Runs within defined scope and rules, often through platforms such as HackerOne or Bugcrowd
Defines scope, safe harbor and payouts
A vulnerability identification method alongside responsible disclosure programs
Business continuity: Planning so critical business functions keep operating during and after a disruption
Broader than disaster recovery: people, processes and facilities, not just IT systems
Disaster recovery focuses on restoring IT systems
Business impact analysis is the key supporting activity
Business email compromise: Targeted social engineering using a compromised or convincingly spoofed trusted email account, often an executive's
Tricks an employee into wiring money, changing payment details or disclosing sensitive information
Often needs no malware at all: just a convincing, well-researched impersonation
Pairs with whaling and invoice-fraud scenarios
Capacity planning: Forecasting and provisioning what is needed to meet future demand
Keeps services available under load, growth and failure
Avoids outages from legitimate overload, which looks like a denial of service
Card skimming: Hidden device on a card reader, ATM or point-of-sale terminal captures card data from the magnetic stripe
Sometimes uses a camera to record the PIN
The data is then used to clone cards
Mitigation: EMV chip cards, tamper-evident seals, regular terminal inspection, contactless or tokenized payments
Certificate: Digital document that binds a public key to an identity, such as a person, server or organization
Issued and digitally signed by a certificate authority
X.509 fields: subject, issuer, public key, validity period
Expired or untrusted certificates cause browser warnings
Certificate authority: Trusted entity that issues, signs and manages digital certificates
Verifies the requestor's identity and forms the root of trust in PKI
Handles issuing, renewing and revoking (CRL or OCSP)
If a CA is compromised, every certificate it issued becomes untrustworthy
Certificate pinning: App accepts only a specific certificate or public key for a given server, not any CA-signed one
Guards against rogue or compromised CAs and on-path attackers presenting fraudulent certificates
Mobile apps commonly pin to defeat TLS interception
Drawback: pinned certificates must be rotated carefully or the app breaks
Chain of custody: Documented, chronological record of who collected, handled, transferred and stored evidence
Shows the evidence was not altered or tampered with from collection through legal proceedings
Must record who, what and when for every handoff
A break in the chain can get evidence ruled inadmissible in court
Chain of trust: Sequence of certificates from a root CA through intermediate CAs down to the end-entity certificate
Each link is validated by the signature of the certificate above it
A missing intermediate certificate can cause trust errors even when the root is valid
Change management: Formal, documented process for proposing, reviewing, approving, implementing and recording IT changes
Minimizes unintended disruption and maintains security and stability
Elements: change request, impact analysis, CAB approval, testing, rollback (backout) plan, documentation
An unauthorized change that skipped the process is a security risk
Checksum: Small fixed-size value calculated from a block of data with a simple algorithm, such as a byte sum or CRC
The receiver recalculates it to detect accidental corruption
Not built to resist deliberate tampering, so weaker than a cryptographic hash
To confirm a file was not maliciously altered, compare a cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 with the vendor's value
For authenticity or non-repudiation, think HMAC or a digital signature instead
CIA triad: Used to evaluate and prioritize security controls
Most scenarios map back to one or more legs of the triad
The opposing DAD framework: disclosure, alteration, denial
Cipher suite: Negotiated set of algorithms two systems agree to use to secure a TLS connection
Includes the key exchange method, the bulk encryption cipher and the message authentication or hash function
Negotiated by client and server during the TLS handshake
Code signing: Applying a digital signature to software with the publisher's private key
Lets recipients verify authenticity and that the code has not been altered since signing
Relies on asymmetric cryptography and a trusted certificate authority
Operating systems block unsigned or tampered software; a failed signature check can signal a supply chain compromise
Cold site: Recovery site with only basic space, power and cooling
The organization brings in hardware, software and data after a disaster
Cheapest option with the longest recovery time; suits non-critical systems or tight budgets
Collision attack: Finds two different inputs that produce the same hash output
Undermines the assumption that a hash value uniquely identifies its data
Targets hash functions, not encryption algorithms
Example: substituting a malicious file with the same digest as a legitimate one, defeating an integrity check
Collision domain: Network segment where devices share the same medium and can interfere if they transmit at once
A hub puts all its ports in one collision domain
Every switch port is its own collision domain; a router has one per interface
Mostly historical (half-duplex Ethernet), but used to contrast hubs and switches
Command and control: Infrastructure and channel (C2) attackers use to send instructions to compromised systems and receive data back
Central to botnets and advanced persistent threat operations
Detected through beaconing traffic to suspicious external domains or IPs
Command injection: Untrusted input is passed to an operating-system shell or command interpreter
Lets the attacker run arbitrary commands with the application's privileges
Related to SQL injection but targets the OS instead of the database
Prevent by avoiding shell calls, using safe APIs, validating and escaping input, and running with least privilege
Community cloud: Cloud shared by several organizations with common requirements, such as compliance or a shared mission
Managed by them or by a third party
Examples: government agencies sharing a compliant cloud, hospitals sharing a healthcare cloud
Costs and responsibilities are split among the members
Compensating control: Alternative control used when the primary or recommended control cannot be implemented
Example: extra monitoring, isolation and strict ACLs for a legacy system that cannot be patched
Used when the standard control is too costly, impractical or technically impossible (legacy, ICS, embedded)
A stand-in, not the preferred solution
Compliance: Meeting the requirements of applicable laws, regulations, standards and contracts
Demonstrated through reporting, monitoring and audits
Consequences of non-compliance: fines, sanctions, reputational damage, loss of license, contractual impacts
Monitoring includes due diligence and due care, attestation and acknowledgement, and automation
Concurrent session usage: Indicator: the same account is active in multiple places or on multiple devices at once
May reveal shared or stolen credentials
Seen in authentication and VPN logs; many systems limit concurrent sessions
Context matters, since legitimate users may use several devices
Confidentiality: Information is not disclosed to unauthorized individuals, entities or processes
One leg of the CIA triad
Preserved by controls such as encryption and access lists
Conflict of interest: Someone, such as a vendor, employee or assessor, has competing interests that could bias their judgment
Example: a consultant recommending products they also sell
One reason for separation of duties and independent audits
Containerization: Packages an application and its dependencies into a lightweight, isolated unit that shares the host OS kernel
Gives consistent, portable deployment without the overhead of a full virtual machine
Lighter than VMs because the kernel is shared
A container escape can expose the underlying host, unlike a VM escape, which affects the hypervisor
Containment: Incident response phase that limits the spread and impact of an incident
Examples: isolating hosts, disabling accounts, blocking malicious IP addresses
Comes after analysis and before eradication
Short-term containment stops damage quickly; long-term containment lets systems run safely until clean-up
Control categories: Four groupings by what a control is made of or who operates it
Technical (technology), managerial (policy and oversight), operational (carried out by people), physical (tangible barriers and devices)
Classify a control twice: category (what kind) and type (what it does)
A firewall is technical and preventive; an awareness program is operational and preventive; a policy is managerial and directive
Control plane: In zero trust, the logical layer where access policies are defined and decisions are made
Houses the Policy Engine, the Policy Administrator, adaptive identity and threat scope reduction
Control types: Six functions: preventive (stop it), deterrent (discourage it), detective (spot it)
Also corrective (fix it afterward), compensating (stand in for a missing control), directive (tell people what to do)
Think by timing: preventive acts before, detective during or after, corrective after the damage
Deterrent influences attackers' behavior, directive influences employees' behavior
One control can fit more than one type, such as a visible CCTV camera (detective and deterrent)
Corrective control: Limits the damage of an incident and restores systems to normal after it has occurred
Examples: restoring from backups, patching after exploitation, incident response, quarantining malware
Patching can be preventive (before an exploit) or corrective (after one), so watch the timing in the question
Credential stuffing: Automatically tries username and password pairs from past breaches against unrelated services
Relies on breach data, not guessing; the credentials are already valid
Mitigation: MFA and unique passwords, often through a password manager
Cryptojacking: Unauthorized use of a victim's computing resources to mine cryptocurrency
Done without the owner's knowledge or consent
Shows up as performance degradation, such as high CPU use and overheating, not data theft
Often delivered through browser scripts or malware
Dark web: Part of the internet reachable only with special software such as Tor
Hosts hidden sites and markets selling stolen credentials, malware and exploits
A threat intelligence source: monitoring can reveal leaked credentials and attacker chatter
Not the same as the deep web, which is just unindexed content such as intranets
Data at rest: Data stored on a persistent medium: disk, database, backup tape or removable drive
Not moving across a network and not being processed in memory
Protect with full-disk, file or database encryption, access controls and secure storage
Classic risk: a stolen laptop or a lost USB stick
Data classification: Organizing data into categories by sensitivity, such as Public, Internal, Confidential and Restricted
Based on the impact if the data is exposed
Drives which controls apply: encryption, access restrictions, retention
Scenarios match data types to the right classification level and controls
Data controller: Under privacy law such as GDPR, the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data
Decides why and how personal data is collected and used
Bears primary legal responsibility for compliance
The processor only acts on the controller's instructions
Data custodian: Role responsible for day-to-day technical handling of data: storage, backup, encryption, recovery
Works to the classification and rules set by the data owner
A hands-on IT or infrastructure role, not the accountable owner
Example duties: backup schedules and access permissions
Data destruction: Physically destroying storage media so data cannot be recovered
Methods: shredding, pulverizing, incineration, degaussing (magnetic media); paper is shredded or pulped
Used when media will not be reused or holds highly sensitive data
Degaussing does not work on SSDs
A certificate of destruction is audit evidence
Data in transit: Data moving between systems across a network: an email, a web request, a file transfer
Protect with TLS, IPsec, VPNs, SSH and WPA3
Main threats: packet sniffing and on-path attacks
Data in use: Data actively being processed, held in memory, registers or caches
Usually unencrypted at this stage, so the hardest state to protect
Protect with secure enclaves, confidential computing, memory encryption, strong access controls and locked screens
Homomorphic encryption is an emerging option
Data loss prevention: Tools and processes that monitor, detect and block unauthorized transmission or exfiltration of sensitive data
Covers email, USB devices and cloud uploads
Scans for patterns such as credit card or SSN formats, or classification tags
Example: blocking an employee from emailing sensitive files externally
Data masking: Obscures or replaces specific sensitive data elements while preserving the data's format
Example: showing only the last four digits of an SSN
Often used in test or training environments
The answer when developers need realistic-looking data without exposing real customer information
Data owner: Person, typically a senior business role, with ultimate accountability for a set of data
Assigns its classification level and approves who may access or use it
The custodian or steward does the day-to-day handling
Controller and processor are GDPR-style roles, separate from internal governance
Scenarios usually name a business executive, not an IT administrator
Data plane: In zero trust, the layer where actual subject-to-resource traffic flows and is enforced
Contains implicit trust zones, the subject or system being protected, and the Policy Enforcement Point
Contrast with the control plane, which defines the policy
Data processor: Under privacy law such as GDPR, processes personal data only on behalf of a data controller and on its instructions
Does not decide why or how the data is collected
Commonly a cloud or outsourcing vendor in scenarios
Data retention: Keeping data for a defined period to meet legal, regulatory and business needs, then securely disposing of it
Too long raises risk and cost; too short can break the law
Privacy laws push data minimization; sanitize at end of life
Periods come from rules such as tax and financial record requirements
Data sanitization: Removing data from storage media so it cannot be recovered, while the media can be reused
Methods: overwriting, cryptographic erase, secure erase
Different from destruction, which physically destroys the media
A normal delete or quick format does not sanitize
NIST SP 800-88 describes clear, purge and destroy levels
Data sovereignty: Data is subject to the laws and governance of the country where it is collected or stored
Storing data in a foreign data center may bring that country's legal requirements
Data steward: Role focused on the quality, accuracy, context and proper use of data within a business domain
Ensures data is labeled, defined and used according to the data owner's policies
Day-to-day usage and labeling, unlike the custodian's technical storage and backup focus
Both act under the data owner's classification decisions
Data subject: The individual the personal data is about (a GDPR term)
Rights: access, correction, portability and erasure
The right to be forgotten is a data subject right
Not the controller (decides why and how), the processor (acts for the controller) or the DPO
Deauthentication attack: Wireless attack that sends forged deauthentication frames to disconnect clients from an access point
Causes denial of service, or forces reconnection so the attacker can capture the WPA handshake or lure users to an evil twin
Possible because management frames were unauthenticated in older Wi-Fi
802.11w protected management frames, mandatory in WPA3, mitigate it
Decommissioning: Controlled retirement of a system, device or application at end of life
Remove it from inventory and networks, revoke access and certificates, sanitize or destroy stored data
Forgotten, unmanaged systems become attack surface
Document it, often with a certificate of sanitization or destruction
Default credentials: Factory-set usernames and passwords (such as admin/admin) that ship with devices and software
Widely published, so attackers can log in with no hacking at all
Changing them is a core hardening step
IoT devices and network gear are common victims, as in the Mirai botnet
Default gateway: Router address on a device's own subnet that it sends traffic to for destinations on other networks
Without a correct one, a device can reach local devices but not the internet
A rogue DHCP server can hand out a malicious gateway, and ARP poisoning can impersonate the real one
Troubleshooting: local works but the internet does not, so check the gateway
Defense in depth: Layered security strategy with multiple, overlapping controls
If one layer fails, others still protect the asset
Example: firewall plus IDS plus endpoint protection plus training
Detective control: Identifies and signals an incident while it is happening or after, but does not stop it
Examples: IDS, SIEM alerts, log reviews, audits, motion sensors, CCTV
Detect means find it: an IDS is detective, an IPS is preventive
Do not pick detective when the control actually blocks the activity
Deterrent control: Discourages an attacker by raising the perceived risk or effort, without necessarily blocking anything
Examples: warning signs, visible cameras, guards, lighting, publicized penalties
Influences behavior; it does not physically stop anyone
A visible camera can also be detective, and a sign can be directive, so read the wording
Dictionary attack: Password guessing using a curated list of common words, phrases and leaked passwords
Faster but less exhaustive than brute force
Mitigation: strong, complex, non-dictionary passwords and key stretching
Differential backup: Copies all data changed since the last full backup
Grows larger each day until the next full backup
A restore needs only the last full backup plus the most recent differential
Slower and larger than incremental, but a faster restore
Example: after a Sunday full, Wednesday's differential holds everything changed Monday to Wednesday
Digital forensics: Collecting, preserving, analyzing and presenting digital evidence in a legally defensible way
Techniques: disk imaging, memory capture, timeline analysis
Chain of custody, legal hold, order of volatility and write blockers
Hashing proves an image has not changed
Digital signature: Sender's private key signs a hash of a message
Anyone with the sender's public key can verify integrity and authenticity
Process: hash, then sign with the private key; verify with the signer's public key
Directive control: Instructs or compels people to behave in a certain way
Examples: policies, standards, procedures, mandatory signage
Directs behavior rather than technically enforcing it
One of the six control types, alongside preventive, deterrent, detective, corrective and compensating
Directory traversal: Manipulates file path input with sequences such as ../ to reach files outside the intended web root
Can expose configuration files or password stores
Mitigation: input validation, canonicalizing paths, a least-privilege web server, sensitive files outside the web root
Disaster recovery: Process and procedures for restoring IT systems, data and infrastructure after a disruption
Measured by RTO (how long until systems are back) and RPO (how much data loss, in time, is acceptable)
The IT-focused subset of business continuity
Uses backups and recovery sites: hot, warm, cold
Discretionary access control: Owner of a resource decides who gets access and what permissions
Flexible, but less centralized consistency than other models
Common in general-purpose operating systems: standard Windows and Linux file permissions
Contrast MAC, with centrally enforced labels
Disinformation: False information deliberately created and spread to deceive
Aims to manipulate opinion or damage a person's or organization's reputation
Intentional, unlike misinformation, which lacks deceptive intent
Example: coordinated campaigns with fake social media accounts
DNS filtering: Blocks malicious or unwanted domains at the DNS resolution step, so the connection is never made
Uses threat intelligence and category lists
Works for every device using the filtering resolver and stops many phishing and malware domains early
Can be bypassed by DNS over HTTPS or other resolvers unless controlled
DNS poisoning: Inserts forged DNS records into a resolver's cache
Users asking for a legitimate domain get the attacker's IP address and land on malicious sites
Also called DNS cache poisoning; behind many pharming attacks
Mitigations: DNSSEC, patched resolvers, source port and query ID randomization, DNS filtering
Downgrade attack: Forces a connection to drop a strong, modern protocol for an older, weaker one
Then exploits the weaker protocol's flaws
Classic example: forcing TLS down to an outdated, vulnerable version or cipher suite
Due care: Reasonable, responsible actions an organization takes to protect its assets
Based on what a prudent entity would do in similar circumstances
The follow-through after due diligence: actually implementing the protections the research found necessary
Due diligence: Research and investigation an organization does before making a decision
Example: vetting a vendor's security practices before signing a contract
Due diligence is the research beforehand; due care is following through
Often tested in vendor risk management scenarios
Dumpster diving: Searching discarded trash for sensitive documents, hardware or information
Mitigation: proper shredding and secure disposal policies
Dynamic code analysis: Tests an application for vulnerabilities by running it and observing its actual behavior, inputs and outputs
Does not examine the source code
Catches runtime issues, such as session-handling flaws, that a static review would miss
Complementary to static analysis, not competing
e-Discovery: Identifying, collecting, preserving and producing electronically stored information (ESI)
Done for litigation, regulatory inquiries or investigations
Embedded system: Computer system with a dedicated function built into a larger device
Examples: printer, smart TV, medical device, vehicle controller
Usually runs fixed firmware with limited resources
Challenges: cannot be patched, weak defaults, long lifespans, too little compute for security agents
Encapsulation: Wrapping data in a header (and sometimes a trailer) at each layer as it moves down the stack
Data becomes a segment, then a packet, then a frame, then bits
Layer 4 adds ports, Layer 3 adds IP addresses, Layer 2 adds MAC addresses
Tunneling and VPNs also encapsulate packets inside other packets
Encryption: Converts plaintext into unreadable ciphertext using an algorithm and a key
Only authorized parties with the correct key can reverse it
Core protection for data at rest, in transit and in use
Reversible with a key, unlike hashing, which is one-way
Ephemeral credentials: Short-lived credentials, tokens or certificates created on demand for one task or session
They expire automatically, so no long-term secret is left to steal
Used in PAM, cloud IAM and DevOps
Shrinks the window of exposure and the reliance on static secrets
Eradication: Incident response phase that removes the root cause from the environment
Delete malware, close exploited vulnerabilities, rebuild compromised systems, reset credentials
Comes after containment and before recovery
If the root cause is not removed, the attacker or malware can return
Evil twin: Rogue wireless access point with the same SSID as a legitimate network
Victims connect to it, letting the attacker eavesdrop, capture credentials or launch on-path attacks
A generic rogue AP is just any unauthorized AP
Defenses: WPA3 or 802.1X with certificate validation, WIDS/WIPS, a VPN on public Wi-Fi, user awareness
Exfiltration: Unauthorized transfer or theft of data from a system or network to a location the attacker controls
Typically the final goal of a data breach
Detected through DLP tools watching for unusual outbound transfers
Exploit: Specific code, technique or method that takes advantage of a vulnerability
Proof-of-concept code is the exploit; the flaw it targets is the vulnerability
External audit: Independent examination of an organization's controls by a third party or regulator
Examples: SOC 2 audit, regulatory examination, ISO 27001 certification audit
More credible than internal audits and sometimes legally required; results in an attestation or report
Fail open: System defaults to an unlocked, permissive state when it fails
Prioritizes availability and safety over security
Classic example: fire-exit doors that unlock on power failure
Fail secure: System defaults to a locked-down, denying state when it fails
Example: doors lock on power loss, versus fail open, where they unlock
Failover: Automatic switch to a redundant or standby system the moment the primary fails
The mechanism or event itself; high availability and fault tolerance are the broader goals
Scenario: the primary system goes down and traffic shifts automatically to a backup
False negative: Failure to detect a real threat or vulnerability, so a genuine problem is reported as clean
More dangerous than a false positive because it creates false assurance
Reduce it with layered detection, up-to-date signatures and more than one scanning method
False positive: Alert or scan result reporting a problem that does not exist
Examples: a legitimate file flagged as malware, a vulnerability reported on an already-patched system
Wastes analyst time and causes alert fatigue
Reduce with tuning and credentialed scans; a false negative (a missed real threat) is more dangerous
Fault tolerance: Ability to keep operating properly when one or more components fail
Achieved through redundancy: RAID arrays, redundant power supplies, clustered servers
Redundancy at the component level prevents a single point of failure
Supports, but is distinct from, high availability at the system or service level
Federation: Identity information is trusted and shared across separate organizations or systems
Users reach resources across organizational boundaries with one identity from their home organization
Uses standards like SAML and OpenID Connect
Identity provider authenticates, service provider trusts it; partners share access without duplicate accounts
Fencing: Physical perimeter barrier, typically metal or wire and rated by height
Marks a property boundary and deters or delays unauthorized entry
A deterrent and delaying control, not an absolute barrier
Paired with lighting and guards as part of defense in depth
Fileless malware: Runs in memory and abuses legitimate system tools such as PowerShell or WMI
Writes no executable files to disk, so signature-based antivirus struggles
Often called a living off the land attack
Detect with behavior-based EDR, script logging and PowerShell restrictions
Memory-resident: may vanish at reboot unless persistence (registry keys, scheduled tasks) is added
Firewall: Monitors and controls incoming and outgoing traffic based on predetermined security rules
A barrier between trusted internal networks and untrusted external networks
Placed at network perimeters; scenarios ask which rule to add or change
Full backup: Copies all selected data whether or not it has changed
Takes the longest and uses the most storage
Fastest and simplest restore: everything is in one set
The base for all other types: incremental is changes since the last backup, differential since the last full
Gap analysis: Structured comparison of current controls or posture against a target state, such as a framework or regulation
Identifies specific deficiencies that need remediation
A governance and compliance activity, done before adopting a framework or after an audit
Produces a prioritized list of missing or weak controls; not the same as a tabletop exercise
Geofencing: Uses GPS, Wi-Fi or IP location to define a virtual boundary
Triggers an action when a device enters or leaves: block access, lock a phone, send an alert
Seen in MDM policies, conditional access (deny logins from outside the country) and geographic data restrictions
Weakness: GPS or IP spoofing and VPNs
Geographic dispersion: Placing data centers, backups or recovery sites in separate regions
A single local disaster or outage cannot take down all systems or copies
Distance should exceed the likely disaster radius
Can conflict with data sovereignty requirements
Governance: Overall framework of policies, roles and processes that directs and controls the security program
The umbrella over policies, standards, procedures and guidelines
Governance sets direction; others implement it
Structures include boards, committees and government entities
Guard rail: Predefined constraint built into an automated process that stops actions outside approved, safe boundaries
Applies even if the script or pipeline is told to do it
Automatic policy enforcement in scripts and pipelines
Example: blocking an overly broad deletion before it runs
Hacktivist: Attacker motivated by political, social or ideological beliefs
Uses website defacement, DDoS, doxing and data leaks to promote a cause or embarrass a target
Moderate skill and resources; the motive is philosophical or political
Hardening: Disable unnecessary services, close unused ports, remove default accounts, apply secure configurations, install patches
Proactive and broad: OS, application and network device configuration
Scenarios list hardening actions, such as disabling services or changing default passwords, as the correct fix
Hashing: One-way function that turns input of any size into a fixed-length output
The same input always gives the same output, and it cannot be reversed to recover the data
Used for integrity verification and password storage
Example: SHA-256; unlike encryption, it is not reversible
Heat map: Visual overlay, usually on a floor plan, showing wireless signal strength and coverage with color gradients
Used to find coverage gaps and overlapping access point coverage before finalizing a wireless design
High availability: Design approach that keeps a service accessible for a very high percentage of time
Achieved with redundancy, failover and load balancing working together
Often expressed in nines: 99.9 percent is about 8.76 hours of downtime a year, 99.999 percent about 5 minutes
The overall goal that fault tolerance and failover support
Homomorphic encryption: Lets computations run directly on encrypted data
The encrypted result, once decrypted, matches the same computation on the plaintext
A third party can process data without ever seeing it
An emerging way to protect data in use; computationally expensive, so niche for now
Honeyfile: Fake, enticingly named file, such as passwords.xlsx, planted to lure attackers or insiders
Any attempt to open or copy it triggers an alert
A single decoy document for early detection of unauthorized browsing
Not a whole fake system, unlike a honeypot
Honeynet: Network of multiple interconnected honeypots simulating a whole decoy network
Shows how attackers move laterally and interact across systems
A honeypot scaled up to a whole network, not a single decoy system
Honeypot: Decoy system designed to look like a legitimate, vulnerable target
Attracts attackers so their techniques can be observed without risking production assets
Used for threat research, early detection or distraction
Not a primary defense; its purpose is gathering attacker intelligence
Honeytoken: Fake piece of data, such as a bogus database record, API key or credential
Planted to detect unauthorized access or exfiltration whenever it is used or appears elsewhere
A single fake data element, unlike a honeyfile (a document) or a honeypot (a system)
Any use is a strong indicator of compromise
Hot site: Fully equipped, continuously running duplicate of the primary site with current data
Ready to take over within minutes or hours
Shortest recovery time (near-zero RTO) and highest cost
Warm has hardware ready but needs data restored; cold is space only; choose by RTO, RPO and budget
Hub: Obsolete Layer 1 device that repeats every signal out of every other port
All connected devices see all traffic, in one collision domain and one broadcast domain
Insecure (anyone can sniff everything) and inefficient (collisions)
Unlike a switch, it has no addressing
Hybrid cloud: Combination of public and private cloud (or on-premises) environments connected so data and applications can move between them
Keeps sensitive workloads private while using the public cloud for scale
Considerations: consistent security policy, connectivity (VPN or dedicated links), identity integration, data movement, visibility
Hybrid encryption: Asymmetric encryption exchanges a symmetric session key securely
Symmetric encryption then encrypts the bulk data efficiently
Gets the security of asymmetric key exchange and the speed of symmetric encryption
Pure asymmetric encryption for bulk data is too slow
Identity proofing: Verifying that a person requesting an identity or account is who they claim to be
Typically checks government-issued ID or other evidence
Happens at enrollment, before any credentials are issued or trusted
Different from authentication, which verifies that identity on every later login
Impersonation: Pretending to be a trusted person, such as an executive, IT support technician, delivery driver or vendor
Used to gain information or access, in person, by phone, email or chat
A social engineering technique that exploits authority and trust
Defenses: verification procedures, badges, call-back processes, awareness training
Implicit deny: Default posture: any access request not explicitly permitted by a rule is rejected
The final rule in most ACLs denies all remaining traffic
Matters for firewall and ACL rule-ordering questions
Implicit trust zone: The small, unavoidable space between a Policy Enforcement Point and the resource it protects
Some minimal trust remains there because enforcement cannot happen at literally every point
True zero trust aims to shrink these zones as small as possible
Impossible travel: Indicator: the same account logs in from locations too far apart to travel between in the elapsed time
Suggests stolen credentials or a session used by a remote attacker
Detected by identity protection tools, SIEM and UEBA; VPNs and proxies can cause false positives
Response: force a password reset, revoke sessions, require MFA
Incident response: Structured approach to preparing for, detecting, containing, eradicating and recovering from security incidents
Phases: preparation, identification, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned
Scenarios give a situation and ask which phase it is: isolating an infected host is containment
Incremental backup: Copies only data changed since the last backup of any type
A restore needs the last full backup plus every incremental in order
Example: a Friday failure needs the Sunday full plus Monday to Thursday incrementals
Indicator of compromise: Forensic evidence suggesting a system has been breached
Examples: file hashes, known-bad IP or domain addresses, registry changes, unusual outbound traffic, unexpected account activity
Used to detect and confirm an intrusion
Often fed from threat intelligence sources
Indicators of malicious activity: Observable signs that a system or account may be compromised or under attack
Examples: impossible travel, unusual resource consumption, concurrent sessions, out-of-cycle logging
Also: missing logs, account lockouts, blocked content
Many are found through SIEM correlation and UEBA
An IoC is a specific artifact, such as a hash or IP; these are broader behaviors
Inherent risk: Risk that exists before any controls or mitigations are applied
The raw exposure of an asset or process to a threat
An assessment starts here, applies controls, then measures what remains
Input validation: Checks all data from users or external systems against expected format, length, type and range before processing
Rejects anything that does not conform
The primary defense against injection attacks, such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting
Malicious payloads rely on an application trusting unchecked input
Insider threat: Risk that originates inside the organization
A current or former employee, contractor or business partner misusing legitimate access
Malicious insiders act intentionally; negligent ones act accidentally
Mitigation: least privilege, monitoring, offboarding procedures
Integrity: Assurance that data has not been altered or tampered with in an unauthorized way
From creation through storage and transmission
Supported by hashing and file integrity monitoring
Integrity controls typically detect modification rather than prevent it
Intellectual property: Creations of the mind with legal ownership: patents, copyrights, trademarks, source code, designs
Theft or leakage causes competitive and legal harm
A frequent nation-state and insider motive
Protect with data classification, DLP, access controls and legal tools such as NDAs
Trade secrets are protected by secrecy
Internal audit: Examination of an organization's controls, processes and compliance by its own staff or audit committee
Used to find gaps and prepare for external audits
Less independent than an external audit but valuable for readiness
IP address: Logical address of a device on a network: 32-bit IPv4 (192.168.1.25) or 128-bit IPv6
Used at Layer 3 to route packets across networks
Has a network part and a host part, separated by the subnet mask
Can be spoofed; defenses include ingress and egress filtering and DHCP snooping with IP source guard
Isolation: Separating a system, process or user from the rest of the environment so a compromise or failure cannot spread
Examples: quarantining an infected host, sandboxes, air gaps, dedicated VLANs
A mitigation technique and an incident response containment action
Related to sandboxing, segmentation and air-gapped networks
Jailbreaking: Removing a mobile device manufacturer's software restrictions to gain root-level or administrative control
Disables built-in protections such as sandboxing and code-signing restrictions
MDM solutions check for and block jailbroken devices before granting access to corporate resources
Journaling: File system or database writes intended changes to a log (the journal) before applying them
After a crash or power loss it can replay or roll back incomplete operations to a consistent state
Gives integrity and fast recovery: NTFS, ext4, database transaction logs
Jump server: Hardened, tightly monitored intermediary that administrators must connect through to reach a more sensitive or isolated segment
Centralizes and logs all administrative access through one hardened chokepoint
Avoids exposing every internal device's management interface directly to administrators' workstations
Just-in-time access: Grants elevated or privileged permissions only for a limited time window, for a specific task
Ties to least privilege and privileged access management
Kerberos: Ticket-based network authentication protocol, the default in Windows Active Directory domains
Client proves identity once to the KDC and receives a TGT, then presents it to get service tickets
The password never crosses the network again, and both sides authenticate each other (mutual authentication)
Uses port 88; needs synchronized clocks (default tolerance 5 minutes), so clock skew is a classic failure
Not RADIUS or TACACS+, which handle network access and device administration
Key escrow: Copies of cryptographic keys held in trust by a third party
Allows authorized recovery of encrypted data under defined conditions
Benefit: recovery if an employee loses their key or leaves
Risk: a compromised escrow agent exposes the keys
Key exchange: Method or protocol that lets two parties establish a shared secret key over an untrusted channel
The key itself is never transmitted
Example: Diffie-Hellman (DHE or ECDHE), the standard in TLS
With ephemeral keys it underpins perfect forward secrecy
Key length: Size of a cryptographic key in bits
Longer keys mean a larger keyspace and harder brute force, at a CPU cost
Strength also depends on the algorithm: a 256-bit ECC key is roughly as strong as a 3072-bit RSA key
Typical minimums: AES-128 or AES-256, RSA 2048 or more (3072+ preferred), ECC 256 or more
Do not compare bit lengths across algorithm families
Key risk indicator: Metric that signals rising exposure to risk before an incident occurs
Examples: unpatched critical systems, failed logins, overdue access reviews
Used in risk reporting and monitoring, with defined thresholds
Not a KPI, which measures performance rather than rising risk
Key stretching: Repeatedly processes a password or key through a hashing algorithm, or uses an intentionally resource-intensive function
Slows down brute-force and dictionary attacks
Paired with salting as password-storage best practice
Keylogger: Spyware that records every keystroke a user types
Used to capture passwords, credit card numbers and other sensitive input
Exists as software and as hardware, such as a device plugged between keyboard and computer
Known environment: White box penetration test: the tester gets full knowledge of the target
Includes network diagrams, source code and credentials
Efficient and thorough; mimics an insider or an attacker who already gathered information
Compare partially known (gray box) and unknown (black box)
Lateral movement: Moving through a network from one compromised system to another after initial access
Searching for additional resources or higher-value targets
A post-exploitation technique that often precedes data exfiltration
Layer 3 switch: Switch that can also route between VLANs or subnets at high speed in hardware
Combines Layer 2 switching and Layer 3 routing in one device
Common in enterprise cores for inter-VLAN routing, usually with ACLs between VLANs
A regular Layer 2 switch cannot route between networks
Least privilege: Grant users, processes or systems only the minimum access rights needed for their job
Over-privileged accounts are the scenario clue
The fix is reducing permissions to the minimum required
Legal hold: Legal obligation to preserve all relevant information, including electronic records
Applies when litigation, investigation or audit is reasonably anticipated
Suspends normal retention and destruction schedules, such as auto-deleting old email
Applies regardless of the usual schedule
Lessons learned: Post-incident review of what happened, how well the response worked and what to improve
Includes root cause analysis and a written report
The final phase of incident response; hold it soon after, in a blameless way
Lighting: Illumination around a facility's exterior and entrances
Deters intruders by removing hiding spots
Improves the effectiveness of guards and cameras after dark
A low-cost deterrent listed with fencing and bollards
Load balancing: Distributes network or application traffic across multiple servers
Optimizes resource use and throughput, cuts response time, avoids overloading one server
Also supports high availability and fault tolerance: if one server fails, traffic goes to healthy ones
Common algorithms: round robin and least connections
Log aggregation: Collecting logs from many systems into one central repository
So they can be searched, correlated and retained, usually with a SIEM or log management platform
The foundation of SIEM detection and investigations
Also protects logs from tampering on a compromised host
Logic bomb: Malicious code inserted into a system that stays dormant until a specific condition triggers it
Triggers include a date or an event
Example: triggered when a termination date appears in HR records
MAC address: 48-bit hardware address, written as six pairs of hex digits such as 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E
Assigned to a network interface and used at Layer 2 to deliver frames on the local network
Switches use MAC addresses; routers use IP addresses
Attacks: MAC spoofing (impersonating a device) and MAC flooding (overflowing a switch table)
MAC filtering is weak because addresses are easy to copy; port security limits MACs per port
MAC flooding: Floods a switch with frames carrying fake source MAC addresses
Overflows the CAM table, so the switch fails open and broadcasts traffic out of all ports
The attacker can then sniff that traffic
Mitigation: port security (limit MAC addresses per port) and sticky MAC
A Layer 2 attack, grouped with ARP poisoning and VLAN hopping
Maintenance window: Scheduled period, usually during low usage, when planned changes, patching and maintenance are allowed
Minimizes disruption to users and the business
Changes must be scheduled within an approved window, with downtime communicated to stakeholders
A business process element of change control
Malicious update: Attacker compromises a software update mechanism or vendor build process
Delivers malware inside what looks like a legitimate patch
Mitigate with code signing and signature verification, hash checks, staged rollouts and vendor risk management
Malware: Any software intentionally designed to cause damage, disrupt operations or gain unauthorized access
Ransomware, spyware and rootkits are subcategories
Man-in-the-middle attack: Attacker secretly intercepts, and may alter, communication between two parties who think they are talking directly
CompTIA now calls it an on-path attack
Examples: rogue access points, ARP spoofing, SSL stripping
Mitigations: strong encryption and certificate validation
Managerial control: Governs how security is planned, organized and overseen
Examples: policies, risk assessments, security planning, vendor reviews, audits
Paperwork and oversight; many are directive (policies) or detective (audits)
Not operational controls, which staff carry out day to day
Mandatory access control: A central authority assigns data classification labels, such as Confidential or Top Secret
Access is granted only if the user's clearance matches or exceeds the label
Users cannot change permissions at all; only a central administrator or the system enforces it
Used in high-security military and government environments, such as SELinux
Memory injection: Inserts malicious instructions into the memory space of a running, legitimate process
The process runs the attacker's code under its own trusted identity and privileges
Evades antivirus that only scans files on disk, because the code never exists as its own file
Metadata: Examples: file creation and modification times, authorship, GPS coordinates in photos (EXIF), email headers
Valuable in investigations, and can leak sensitive information
Has forensic and OSINT value; scrub it before publishing documents
Microsegmentation: Granular network segmentation down to the individual workload or application level
Common in virtualized and cloud environments, often through software-defined networking
Fine-grained east-west traffic control, beyond what VLAN-based segmentation offers
Microservices: Structures an application as small, independently deployable services, each handling one business function
Services talk over well-defined APIs, often REST or messaging
Benefit: fault isolation and independent scaling and patching
Drawback: a larger attack surface, since every service and interface must be authenticated and secured
Misconfiguration: Incorrect or insecure settings in software, devices or cloud services
Examples: open storage buckets, default accounts, unnecessary services, overly broad permissions
One of the most common causes of breaches
Prevent with secure baselines, configuration scanning, infrastructure as code and change control
Misinformation: False or inaccurate information spread whether or not the person sharing it means to deceive
Can still damage trust, cause panic or influence decisions
Disinformation, by contrast, is deliberately false and meant to deceive
Missing logs: Gaps, or cleared or deleted entries, in log files
Often a sign that an attacker or insider is covering their tracks
Logging pipelines can also fail for benign reasons, so investigate gaps
Protect logs with centralized aggregation (SIEM), write-once storage and integrity monitoring
Multi-cloud: Using services from more than one cloud provider
Avoids lock-in, improves resilience and picks the best service for each need
Cost: more complexity in security, identity and visibility
Needs consistent IAM, policy and monitoring across providers, often with a CASB
Multifactor authentication: Requires two or more independent factors from different categories
Categories: something you know, something you have, something you are, somewhere you are
Two items from the same category, such as a password plus a PIN, is not true MFA
Scenarios test valid versus invalid factor combinations
Nation-state actor: Threat actor sponsored or directed by a government
Large budgets, advanced tools and patience
Goals: espionage, sabotage of critical infrastructure, political or military advantage
Often runs advanced persistent threat campaigns; the highest resources and sophistication of any actor
Need to know: Limits access to information to those whose job duties require it
Applies even if they already hold sufficient clearance
Information-specific, unlike least privilege, which is about access rights
Often tested with classified data handling
Network port: Number from 0 to 65,535 that identifies a specific service or application on a device
Makes incoming traffic reach the right program
IP address plus port is a socket; ports 0 to 1023 are the well-known ports
Open ports are attack surface; a port scan reports each port as open, closed or filtered
Network segmentation: Dividing a network into smaller, isolated subnetworks, typically with VLANs or firewalls
Contains breaches, reduces the attack surface and enforces access control between zones
A core defense-in-depth and containment strategy, paired with least privilege
Example: isolating payment processing or SCADA from the general network
Network tap: Hardware device inserted inline on a physical link that passively copies all passing traffic to a monitoring port
Gives full visibility without affecting the original data flow
More reliable than port mirroring: full line rate, even malformed packets
Often used for IDS or IPS sensor placement
Non-repudiation: Assurance that an entity cannot deny having performed an action, such as sending a message or completing a transaction
Provided by digital signatures and audit logs
Prevents a sender from denying authorship
Nonce: A number used once: a value that must never repeat with the same key
Makes every encryption or authentication operation unique
Identical plaintexts give different ciphertexts, and captured messages cannot be replayed
Reusing a nonce with the same key in counter mode or GCM can completely break confidentiality
In challenge-response authentication, a fresh random value defeats replay attacks
Obfuscation: Deliberately making code, data or communications hard to understand or analyze
Used to evade detection or reverse engineering
Malware authors use it to evade signature-based detection
Different from steganography, which hides the existence of data rather than just making it unreadable
On-premises: Infrastructure an organization owns and operates in its own facilities
Full control over hardware and data, but full responsibility for security, maintenance, power and capacity
Contrast with cloud: highest control, higher capital cost, slower scaling
Responsible for the entire stack, including physical security
Onboarding and offboarding: Onboarding brings new staff in: accounts, access, equipment, training, policy acknowledgment
Offboarding removes access and recovers assets when they leave
Offboarding must revoke access immediately, recover devices and review data
Open public ledger: Distributed, transparent record of transactions replicated across many nodes and visible to all participants
New entries are validated by consensus, not a single central authority
The foundational structure behind most blockchains
Integrity comes from decentralization and consensus: hard for any one party to secretly alter past records
Operational control: Carried out day to day by people rather than by technology
Examples: security awareness training, guard patrols, change and patch procedures, incident response drills
Most often confused with managerial controls (policy and oversight)
Training programs and routine procedures are the classic examples
Operational security: OPSEC: identify information adversaries could piece together, then protect it
Habits: not oversharing on social media, clean desk practices, controlling who needs to know what
Protect small pieces of information that reveal larger secrets
Order of volatility: Sequence for collecting digital evidence, from the most volatile (lost fastest) to the least
CPU registers and cache, RAM, swap, disk, remote logs and monitoring data, then archival media and backups
Collect the most volatile first: memory before disk
Organized crime: Structured criminal groups that run cyber attacks as a business
Activities: ransomware, business email compromise, credential theft, carding, extortion, selling stolen data or access
More resources than hacktivists, generally fewer than nation-states
Out-of-cycle logging: Log entries or activity at unusual times or outside normal patterns
Examples: an administrator logging in at 3 a.m., a scheduled job running at an odd hour
Baselines of normal behavior make it detectable
Investigate for stolen accounts and insider threats
Packet filtering: Basic firewall technique inspecting individual packet headers: source and destination IP, port, protocol
Compares each packet to a static rule set and allows or denies it independently, with no connection state
Simplest and fastest, but least secure: it cannot see connection context or payload content
Partially known environment: Gray box penetration test: the tester gets limited information
Examples: a normal user account or part of the network layout
Simulates a malicious insider or an attacker who already has a foothold
Pass-the-hash: Attacker captures a hashed password and uses it directly to authenticate
No need to crack it into plaintext
Works because some authentication protocols accept the hash itself as proof of identity
Enables lateral movement without the actual password
Passive reconnaissance: Gathering information about a target without interacting with its systems
Sources: OSINT, WHOIS, DNS records, social media, job postings, search engines like Shodan
Hard for the target to detect
Contrast active reconnaissance, which touches the target
Password manager: Generates, stores and fills strong, unique passwords for each account
Protected by one strong master password, ideally with MFA
Users do not reuse or memorize passwords
A best-practice defense against credential stuffing and password reuse
Risk: a single point of compromise, so protect the master password with MFA
Password policy: Rules governing how passwords are created and managed
Settings: minimum length, complexity, history (reuse), maximum and minimum age, lockout threshold, storage
Modern NIST guidance favors length and breached-password blocklists over forced complexity and routine expiry
Password spraying: Tries one commonly used password, such as Spring2024!, against many different accounts
Opposite of a dictionary attack, which tries many passwords against a single account
Password vaulting: Stores privileged and shared credentials in an encrypted vault
Users must check credentials out; access is logged, passwords rotate automatically and sessions may be recorded
A core privileged access management feature, alongside just-in-time access and ephemeral credentials
Prevents sharing and hard-coding of administrator passwords
Passwordless authentication: Verifies identity with a factor other than a memorized password
Examples: a biometric scan, a hardware security key, a certificate on a trusted device
Relies on possession or biometric factors
Removes password-based risks: brute force, dictionary and credential stuffing attacks
Patch management: Systematic process of identifying, testing, acquiring and deploying software updates that fix vulnerabilities and bugs
Governed by policy that balances security urgency against system stability
Lifecycle: identify, test in a non-production environment, deploy, verify
Emergency or out-of-band patching applies to actively exploited zero-days
Penetration testing: Authorized, simulated attack by security professionals
Actively exploits identified vulnerabilities to show real-world exploitability and impact, beyond mere detection
Knowledge levels: black box, white box, gray box
Rules of engagement and written authorization are critical
Perfect forward secrecy: Each session uses a unique ephemeral key
Even if the server's long-term private key is compromised later, past captured sessions cannot be decrypted
Achieved with ephemeral Diffie-Hellman: DHE or ECDHE
Persistence: Techniques attackers use to keep long-term access to a compromised system
Survives reboots, credential changes and initial detection attempts
Examples: scheduled tasks, registry run keys, new admin accounts
Closely tied to advanced persistent threat behavior
Pharming: Silently redirects users from a legitimate website to a fraudulent one
Done by poisoning DNS or altering a hosts file
Victims reach the fake site even when they type the correct address
Unlike phishing, no lure or click is required
Defenses: DNSSEC, secure DNS, endpoint protection, checking certificates
Phishing: Social engineering using fraudulent emails or messages, often impersonating a trusted source
Tricks victims into revealing information or installing malware
The most commonly tested social engineering attack
Variants differ by target and medium: spear phishing, whaling, vishing, smishing
Phishing simulation: Controlled exercise sending fake phishing messages to employees
Measures how many click or report them
Part of awareness campaigns; track click and report rates and use results for learning, not punishment
Physical control: Tangible barrier or device that protects facilities, equipment and people
Examples: locks, fences, bollards, badge readers, access control vestibules, cameras, lighting, guards
Types: locks and bollards are preventive, cameras and motion sensors detective, signs and visible guards deterrent
Physical security sensors: Detect physical presence, motion or pressure to trigger alarms, lighting or recording
Infrared (PIR) detects body heat; pressure detects weight on a floor or mat
Microwave detects motion from reflected microwave energy and can see through thin walls
Ultrasonic detects motion from reflected sound waves
Pivoting: Post-exploitation technique: using a compromised system as a relay point
Reaches and attacks other systems that would otherwise be unreachable
Uses a foothold device to bridge into isolated or segmented network zones
Different from lateral movement between peer systems
Plaintext and ciphertext: Plaintext is data in readable, unencrypted form
Ciphertext is the unreadable result of applying an encryption algorithm and key
Decryption reverses it with the correct key
A hash is not ciphertext, because it cannot be reversed
Platform diversity: Using different operating systems, hardware vendors, software and technologies across the environment
A single vulnerability or failure does not affect every system
Trade-off: higher complexity and cost; also called technology diversity
Playbook: Documented set of conditional steps and decision points guiding a team through a specific type of incident
Covers who does what and under which conditions
The human-readable decision tree: what to do and when
A runbook is the step-by-step technical procedure that carries the steps out
Policy Administrator: Takes the Policy Engine's decision and generates session-specific instructions or credentials
Establishes or tears down the communication path at the Policy Enforcement Point
Pairs with the Policy Engine: the Engine decides, the Administrator communicates the decision
Policy Enforcement Point: Zero trust data-plane component acting as the gatekeeper
Allows, monitors or terminates the connection between a subject and a resource
Acts strictly on the decision handed down by the Policy Administrator
Sits in the data plane and enforces; the Policy Engine and Administrator in the control plane decide
Policy Engine: Zero trust control-plane component that evaluates an access request
Weighs policy rules, threat intelligence and context about the subject and device
Renders the grant, deny or revoke decision
The component that decides; the Policy Enforcement Point enforces
Port mirroring: Switch feature, also called SPAN, that copies traffic from source ports to a destination port for monitoring
Lets analysis tools observe traffic without a dedicated inline tap
A switch-configuration alternative to a network tap
Can drop packets under heavy load, since it competes for switch processing resources
Port security: Switch feature that restricts which devices can use a port
Limits the number of MAC addresses, or specifies the allowed ones
Shuts down or restricts the port when the rule is violated
Defends against MAC flooding and unauthorized devices; sticky MAC and violation modes (shutdown, restrict, protect)
Related to 802.1X and NAC; disable unused switch ports
Pretexting: Social engineering using a fabricated, believable scenario or false identity
Manipulates a victim into divulging information or granting access
Builds trust before the actual request
Example: posing as an auditor or a new vendor
Preventive control: Stops an incident from happening in the first place by blocking or avoiding the threat
Examples: firewalls, locks, least privilege, encryption, MFA, patching, training
Prevent means stop it before it happens
If a control only alerts, it is detective, not preventive
Exam examples: firewall rules, inline IPS, door locks, bollards, access control vestibules, account lockout
Privacy: Protecting personal information from unauthorized collection, use or disclosure
Respects an individual's right to control their own data
Tied to regulations and roles like data controller and data processor
Concerns personal data rights; confidentiality concerns general information protection
Private cloud: Cloud environment used by a single organization
Hosted on its own premises or by a provider
More control, customization and isolation, at higher cost
Often chosen for regulated data; the organization carries more of the operational and security responsibility
Private key: Secret half of an asymmetric key pair that must be protected and never shared
Decrypts data encrypted with the matching public key
If compromised, communications and signatures tied to it become untrustworthy and the certificate must be revoked
Often stored in hardware such as a TPM or HSM
Privilege escalation: Exploiting a vulnerability, design flaw or misconfiguration to gain more access than originally granted
Vertical: gaining higher-level rights, such as user to admin
Horizontal: accessing another user's same-level data
Proxy server: Intermediary between clients and external servers that forwards requests and responses on their behalf
Can provide caching, content filtering, anonymity and an extra layer of inspection
Forward proxy: protects and controls internal clients accessing the internet
Reverse proxy: protects and distributes load for internal servers receiving external requests
Public cloud: A provider such as AWS, Azure or Google Cloud owns and operates shared, multi-tenant infrastructure
Delivered to many customers over the internet
Lowest upfront cost and high scalability
Shared responsibility model; data sovereignty and tenant isolation are common concerns
Public key: Openly shareable half of an asymmetric key pair
Others use it to encrypt data meant for the key owner
Verifies a digital signature made with the matching private key
Distributed freely, often through a certificate
Purple team: Collaborative function where red and blue team members share techniques, findings and insights in real time
Aims to improve detection and response faster than siloed exercises
Not a separate standing team but an approach bridging red and blue
The one that maximizes knowledge transfer between attackers and defenders
Qualitative risk analysis: Rates risks with descriptive categories such as high, medium and low
Based on expert judgment, not numbers
Fast and cheap but subjective; contrast quantitative analysis, with SLE, ARO and ALE
Quantitative risk analysis: Uses numerical values and formulas to estimate expected financial loss from risks
SLE = AV x EF and ALE = SLE x ARO
Compares expected loss with the cost of controls
Needs good data; justifies security spending by showing a control costs less than the loss it prevents
Quantum cryptography: Cryptography using quantum mechanical properties, such as photon polarization in quantum key distribution
Or cryptography designed to resist attacks from quantum computers
Quantum computing is an emerging threat that can break current asymmetric algorithms like RSA
Mitigation: move to quantum-resistant (post-quantum) algorithms before that capability matures
Quarantine: Isolating a suspicious file, device or message in a restricted area
It cannot harm other systems while it is investigated or cleaned
Used by antivirus, email gateways and NAC, where non-compliant devices go to a remediation VLAN
Race condition: Vulnerability where the outcome depends on the timing or sequence of two or more operations
The attacker manipulates the gap between them to get an unintended result
Classic example: TOCTOU, time-of-check to time-of-use
The attacker changes a resource's state between the check and the use
Fix: make the check-then-act sequence atomic
Rainbow table: Large pre-computed lookup table of password hashes and the plaintexts that produce them
Reverses unsalted hashes almost instantly instead of computing each guess
Used for offline cracking of stolen hashes
Defeat it with a unique salt per password, plus key stretching such as bcrypt or PBKDF2
Ransomware: Malware that encrypts a victim's files or locks their system
Demands payment, usually in cryptocurrency, to restore access
Double extortion: encryption plus a threat to leak the data
Recommendation: keep offline backups rather than pay the ransom
Red team: Security professionals who simulate real-world adversary tactics, techniques and procedures
Run in an authorized offensive exercise to test detection and response
Represents offense; blue is defense; purple is collaboration between both
