Redundancy: Duplicating critical components so the failure of one does not cause an outage
Examples: disks, power supplies, network links, servers, sites
A core availability concept: RAID, dual power supplies, NIC teaming, clustering, multiple ISPs
Regulated data: Data whose handling is controlled by law, regulation or industry standard
Examples: PII, PHI, payment card data
Matching regimes: PHI is HIPAA, cardholder data is PCI DSS, EU residents' personal data is GDPR, financial reporting data is SOX
Mishandling brings fines and legal action; usually needs stricter classification, encryption and retention rules
Replay attack: A valid data transmission, such as an authentication token or session packet, is intercepted and retransmitted
Tricks the receiver into granting access or repeating an action
Classic scenario: a captured login packet resent later
Mitigated with timestamps, sequence numbers, session tokens and nonces
Replication: Continuously or periodically copying data from one system or site to another
Keeps a current duplicate available, improving availability
Synchronous waits for the copy (zero data loss, needs low latency); asynchronous lags slightly (small data loss possible)
Not a backup: it also copies corruption, ransomware and deletions
Residual risk: Risk that remains after controls and mitigations are applied
Must be within the organization's risk appetite and tolerance, or explicitly accepted by the risk owner
Inherent risk reduced by the effectiveness of controls equals residual risk
Resource reuse: Memory, storage or other resources released by one tenant are reassigned to another without being fully cleared
Mitigate by zeroing memory and wiping storage on release, encrypting volumes, and strong tenant isolation
Responsibility matrix: Documented breakdown of which security tasks a cloud provider handles and which the customer handles
Also called the shared responsibility model
The split varies by service: IaaS, PaaS or SaaS
The customer's share grows from SaaS to PaaS to IaaS, since the provider manages less of the stack
Scenarios ask who is responsible for a specific failure, such as a misconfigured setting
Responsible disclosure: Researcher privately reports a discovered vulnerability to the vendor
Gives time to fix it before details are published, so users are protected
Many organizations publish a disclosure policy so researchers know how to report
RFID cloning: Copying data from an RFID badge or tag onto another card so the clone can open doors
Low-frequency proximity cards often have no encryption, so they can be read from a short distance
Mitigations: encrypted smart cards, RFID-blocking sleeves, MFA at sensitive doors, monitoring badge logs
Right to be forgotten: Privacy right, codified in regulations like GDPR (the right to erasure)
Individuals can request erasure of their personal data when it is no longer necessary, consent is withdrawn, or processing was unlawful
Organizations need a documented process to verify and honor requests
Right-to-audit clause: Contract provision that lets a customer audit a vendor's security controls, processes and compliance
Directly, or through an independent assessor
A key third-party risk control, often written into master service agreements
Risk: Potential for loss or damage when a threat exploits a vulnerability
The combination of threat and vulnerability, not either alone
Assessed qualitatively or quantitatively, for example with annualized loss expectancy
Risk acceptance: Knowingly tolerating a risk without further treatment
Usually because the cost of controls exceeds the potential loss, or the risk is within tolerance
Document it as an exception or exemption approved by the risk owner
A conscious, documented decision within risk appetite, not simply ignoring the risk
Risk appetite: General amount and type of risk an organization is willing to pursue or accept to achieve its objectives
Set by senior leadership as a broad, strategic statement
Risk tolerance is different: specific and measurable for one risk
Risk assessment: Identifying risks to assets, analyzing their likelihood and impact, and evaluating them to decide how to respond
Can be ad hoc, recurring, one-time or continuous
Qualitative versus quantitative analysis; formulas SLE, ARO, ALE
Outputs feed the risk register and the choice of risk response
Risk avoidance: Eliminating a risk by not doing the activity that creates it
Examples: discontinuing a product, avoiding a market, shutting down a vulnerable service
The only response that removes the risk completely, but it may remove business value too
Risk management: Identifying, assessing and responding to risks to reduce their impact on the organization
Four responses: avoidance, transference, mitigation, acceptance
Scenarios ask which strategy is described
Risk is likelihood multiplied by impact
Risk mitigation: Reducing the likelihood or impact of a risk with controls
Examples: patching, segmentation, encryption, training, monitoring
Continue until the residual risk is acceptable
The most common risk response; controls can be preventive, detective or corrective
Risk register: Documented, centralized log of identified risks
Records each risk's description, likelihood, impact, owner, current controls and treatment status
A living document tracked over time
Distinct from a one-time risk assessment report
Risk tolerance: Specific, measurable degree of variance an organization will accept around a particular risk or objective
Turns the broader risk appetite into concrete thresholds
Tolerance is specific and measurable; appetite is the broad strategic attitude it comes from
A classic distractor pair on the exam
Risk transference: Shifting the financial impact of a risk to a third party
Examples: cyber insurance, outsourcing, contractual indemnification
Responsibility and reputational harm usually stay with the organization
One of four responses: avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept
Rogue access point: Wireless access point connected to a network without authorization
Planted by an attacker or installed by a well-meaning employee
Creates an unmonitored back door around the perimeter
Detect with WIDS/WIPS and wireless surveys; prevent with 802.1X and port security
An evil twin is a special case that imitates a legitimate SSID
Role-based access control: Assigns permissions to users by job role instead of individually
Simplifies administration as users are added, moved or removed
The most common enterprise access model
Tied to least privilege and separation of duties
Clue: permissions described as tied to job function or title
Root of trust: Foundational, inherently trusted hardware, firmware or cryptographic component, such as a TPM
The anchor from which an entire chain of trust is built
Used to verify that each later layer of boot code or software has not been tampered with
Ties to secure boot and attestation; it must itself be trustworthy
Rootkit: Malware that gains and keeps privileged (root or administrator) access
Actively hides its presence from users and security tools
Operates at a low level, such as kernel mode, to evade detection
Often needs specialized tools or a full OS reinstall to remove
Router: Layer 3 device that connects different networks and forwards packets between them
Reads the destination IP address and picks the best next hop from its routing table
Does not forward broadcasts, so it separates broadcast domains
Usually the default gateway; may also do NAT, ACL filtering and VPN termination
Hardening: change defaults, disable unused services, restrict management with ACLs, filter spoofed addresses, authenticate routing updates
Routing table: List of networks a router knows about, with the next hop or interface to reach each
Matches the destination IP to the most specific entry
A default route (0.0.0.0/0) catches everything else
Entries come from connected networks, static routes or dynamic protocols such as OSPF and BGP
Forged updates and route hijacking attack it: authenticate routing protocols and filter accepted routes
Rule-based access control: Grants or restricts access by predefined, system-enforced rules, often if-then logic
Applied uniformly, regardless of the user's identity or role
Not role-based access control, even though both are casually abbreviated RBAC
Rules of engagement: Written agreement setting scope, permitted techniques, timing, targets and authorization for a pen test or red team exercise
Never test without it: it is the permission slip
Limits legal liability and prevents damage
Includes emergency contacts and what is out of scope
Runbook: Detailed, step-by-step technical instructions, often automated or scripted, for a specific task or response action
Carries the action out consistently every time
The concrete execution layer, such as the exact steps that isolate a host and collect forensic artifacts
A playbook is the higher-level decision logic that decides when to trigger it
Salting: Adding a unique random value to data, typically a password, before hashing it
Identical inputs produce different hash outputs
Explains why two users with the same password have different stored hashes
Used alongside hashing, not instead of it
Sandboxing: Running an untrusted application, file or code in an isolated environment
Separated from the host system and production network, so malicious behavior cannot affect the real environment
Malware analysis: safely detonating a suspicious file
Scalability and elasticity: Scalability: handling a growing workload by adding resources
Elasticity: adding and removing resources automatically as demand rises and falls
Elasticity is automatic and dynamic; scalability is the capacity to grow
Cloud platforms are valued for both
Screened subnet: Network segment, formerly called a DMZ, between the internet and the internal network
Hosts public-facing servers such as web, mail and DNS, so a compromise does not give direct access to the internal LAN
Placement: internet, external firewall, screened subnet, internal firewall, internal LAN
Secure baseline: Documented minimum set of security configurations a system must be brought to and kept at
A lifecycle: establish the standard, deploy it consistently to new systems, maintain it over time
More than a one-time baseline configuration snapshot used only for drift detection
Secure cookie: Browser cookie marked with attributes such as Secure and HttpOnly
Mitigates session hijacking via cross-site scripting
Secure enclave: Isolated, hardware-based area of a processor that stores and processes sensitive data
Holds encryption keys and biometric templates separately from the main OS
Stays protected even if the OS is compromised
Similar purpose to a TPM, but typically a dedicated secure co-processor on mobile devices and modern CPUs
Security awareness training: Program teaching employees to recognize and respond to threats such as phishing and social engineering, and to follow security policies
Initial onboarding training plus recurring refreshers
Elements: phishing campaigns, anomalous behavior recognition, user guidance, reporting and monitoring
Security guard: Trained person stationed at a facility to monitor access, verify identities, patrol and respond to incidents in real time
Flexible, judgment-based control that adapts to unexpected situations
Unlike fixed controls such as fencing or badge readers
Adds cost and remains subject to human error and social engineering
Security guideline: Recommended practice that offers advice and flexibility but is not mandatory
Examples: tips for memorable passphrases, choosing a secure Wi-Fi network
Policies and standards are mandatory; guidelines are optional and advisory
Security key: Physical hardware authenticator: a USB, NFC or Bluetooth device
A something-you-have factor and a strong MFA option, such as a YubiKey
Phishing-resistant: it checks the site's origin before responding
Security policy: High-level, management-approved document stating what the organization requires to protect information and systems, and why
Hierarchy: policy (what and why), standard (mandatory specifics), procedure (how, step by step), guideline (optional advice)
Examples: acceptable use, information security, BCP/DR, incident response, data retention
Security procedure: Step-by-step instructions for performing a specific task consistently
Examples: onboarding a user, restoring from backup, responding to a phishing report
Describes how; supports policies and standards
Used for training and audits; sometimes called SOPs or runbooks
Security standard: Specific, mandatory requirement that supports a policy
Examples: minimum password length, approved encryption algorithms, required configuration baselines
Says exactly what level or technology must be used
Procedures say how to do the task; mandatory and specific, such as AES-256 for data at rest, means standard
Security zone: Logical or physical area of a network grouped by trust level and function
Examples: trusted internal, untrusted internet, screened subnet, guest, management
Controls are enforced where zones meet; traffic between zones passes through a firewall
The basis of segmentation and zero trust, which adds implicit trust zones and policy enforcement points
Self-assessment: Organization evaluates its own controls and compliance against a checklist or framework
Usually quick and cheap, with no independent verification
The least objective form of assessment
Common for PCI DSS self-assessment questionnaires and quick gap checks
Self-signed certificate: Digital certificate signed with its own private key, not by a trusted CA
Can enable encryption but gives no third-party validation of identity
Browsers and clients show warnings unless it is manually trusted
Fine for internal labs and development, risky for production or public sites: no chain of trust
Root CA certificates are also self-signed, but are pre-installed in trust stores
Separation of duties: Divides critical tasks among multiple people
No single individual can complete a sensitive process alone
Example: one person requests a payment and another approves it
Fraud prevention; not the same as least privilege
Server-side request forgery: Tricks a server into making HTTP requests to destinations the attacker chooses
Often targets internal-only services or the cloud metadata endpoint
Abuses the server's trust and network position (SSRF)
Mitigation: destination allow lists, blocking internal address ranges, segmentation, cloud metadata protections
Not CSRF, which targets the user's browser
Serverless computing: Cloud model where the provider dynamically allocates and manages the underlying servers
Scales resources up or down automatically
Developers deploy code, often as functions, without provisioning infrastructure
Servers still exist: the provider manages and patches them, and the customer is responsible only for the function code
Session hijacking: Attacker steals or guesses a valid session token (such as a cookie or session ID)
Uses it to impersonate a logged-in user without the password
Related to on-path attacks and XSS
Defenses: TLS everywhere, Secure and HttpOnly cookies, short session lifetimes
Also: re-authenticate for sensitive actions and regenerate tokens after login
Session key: Temporary symmetric key generated for a single communication session and discarded afterward
Established securely with asymmetric cryptography or a Diffie-Hellman exchange
Fast symmetric encryption then protects the actual data: the symmetric half of hybrid encryption such as TLS
Each session has its own key, so compromising one does not expose the others; ephemeral exchange adds perfect forward secrecy
Shadow IT: Hardware, software or cloud services used without the knowledge, approval or oversight of IT or security
Unapproved tools bypass security controls, patching and DLP policies
Creates blind spots the security team cannot monitor or protect
Shoulder surfing: Covertly observing someone's screen, keyboard or written material
Captures sensitive information such as passwords or PINs
Mitigations: privacy screens and awareness training
Side loading: Installing an app from a source other than the device's official, vetted app store
Bypasses the store's security review and malware screening
A mobile vulnerability, distinct from jailbreaking
MDM policies commonly block installs from outside the approved store
Single point of failure: Component whose failure stops the entire system or service because there is no redundancy or alternative path
Examples: a lone firewall, a single internet link, a central automation server, one power feed
Removing them is a core high-availability goal
Fix with redundancy, clustering, load balancing and failover
Single sign-on: Log in once with one set of credentials and reach multiple independent applications
Improves user experience and centralizes authentication logging
Creates a single point of failure: a compromised SSO credential puts every connected system at risk
Pair it with MFA as the mitigation
Site survey: Physical assessment of a location before deploying wireless access points
Measures signal strength, interference and coverage
Finds dead zones, interference sources and the best access point locations
Performed before or during wireless design; the heat map is its visual output
Situational awareness: Understanding the environment and threats around you
Recognizing unusual people, requests or behavior and knowing how to respond
Examples: noticing tailgating, shoulder surfing or a suspicious email
A user-guidance topic in security awareness; it encourages reporting instead of ignoring
Smart card: Physical authentication token with an embedded microprocessor chip
Securely stores credentials or cryptographic certificates
Used with a PIN: something you have plus something you know, for true MFA
Examples: Common Access Card (CAC) and Personal Identity Verification (PIV) card
Smishing: Social engineering attack delivered by SMS text messages
Tricks recipients into clicking malicious links or revealing information
Often fake delivery notifications or bank alerts
Snapshot: Point-in-time image of a VM, volume or file system that records its state for quick rollback
Usually depends on the original storage, so it is not offsite or independent
Not a substitute for real backups; handy before risky changes
Social engineering: Psychological manipulation that tricks people into divulging confidential information or taking actions that compromise security
Relies on principles of persuasion: authority, urgency, scarcity, social proof
The overarching category covering phishing, vishing, pretexting, impersonation and more
Spear phishing: Targeted phishing aimed at a specific individual or group
Uses personalized information to increase credibility
Generic phishing is mass and untargeted; spear phishing is targeted and researched
Clues: a named recipient or a specific job reference
Spoofing: Forging the identity of a source to impersonate a trusted party or hide the attacker's origin
Forms: IP spoofing (DDoS reflection), email spoofing in phishing, MAC spoofing, caller ID spoofing
Email spoofing is countered by SPF, DKIM and DMARC
Ingress and egress filtering reduce IP spoofing
Spyware: Malware that covertly monitors and collects information about a user's activities without consent
Focused on surveillance and data collection, not destruction
Keyloggers are often categorized as a type of spyware
SSL stripping: Downgrade attack by an on-path attacker
Intercepts the user's initial HTTP request and keeps the victim on unencrypted HTTP while speaking HTTPS to the real server
Mitigated by HSTS and HSTS preload lists, plus users checking for HTTPS
Standard operating procedure: Documented, approved step-by-step instructions for performing a routine operation consistently and safely
In change management, describes how routine changes are carried out
Reduces errors and supports audits and training
Closely related to procedures and runbooks: a repeatable task done the same way every time
Stateful inspection: Firewall technique that tracks the state of active connections, such as TCP handshake status
Decides based on the context of traffic flows, not just individual packets
Return traffic for an established session is permitted automatically, with no separate rule
Static code analysis: Reviews source code for security flaws and coding errors without running the program
Often automated by scanning tools during development
Examines code at rest, before runtime
Catches issues like hardcoded credentials or insecure function calls early
Contrast dynamic analysis, which tests the running application
Steganography: Concealing a message, file or data inside another seemingly innocent file
Example: hiding text inside an image
Hides the existence of the data
Encryption, by contrast, scrambles data but does not hide that it exists
Stream cipher: Symmetric algorithm that encrypts data one bit or byte at a time
Combines data with a pseudorandom keystream
Suited to continuous data such as voice or video
RC4 is a now largely deprecated example
Typically faster than block ciphers, with less error propagation protection
Subnet: Subdivision of an IP network: addresses that share the same network prefix
Written in CIDR notation, such as 192.168.1.0/24
Devices in the same subnet talk directly; other subnets go through a router or firewall
Keeps broadcasts small and lets you apply controls between groups
A /24 is 255.255.255.0 and gives 254 usable hosts
Subnet mask: 32-bit value that marks which part of an IPv4 address is the network and which is the host
Devices use it to decide whether a destination is local or must go to the default gateway
A bigger prefix means a smaller network
Supply chain attack: Targets vulnerabilities in a trusted third-party vendor, supplier or software component
Compromises the systems of their downstream customers
Examples: compromised software updates, hardware tampering before delivery
Switch: Connects devices on the same network and forwards Ethernet frames only to the port where the destination MAC address lives
Learns a MAC address table from the traffic it sees
Layer 2; a Layer 3 switch can also route
Attacks and defenses: MAC flooding and port security, ARP poisoning and DAI, rogue DHCP and DHCP snooping
VLAN hopping, and spanning tree attacks stopped by BPDU Guard
Contrast a hub (repeats to every port) and a router (uses IP addresses between networks)
Symmetric encryption: Uses a single shared secret key to both encrypt and decrypt
Fast, but needs a secure way to distribute the key to all parties
The key-distribution problem is a classic scenario question
Syslog: Standard protocol and message format for sending log events from devices and servers to a central collector
Messages carry facility and severity levels; severity runs from 0 (emergency) to 7 (debug)
Used by network gear and Linux to forward logs to a SIEM
Plain syslog over UDP is unencrypted and unreliable, so use TLS where possible
Tabletop exercise: Discussion-based incident response exercise: stakeholders walk through a simulated scenario verbally
Evaluates and improves plans, roles and decision-making
No systems are touched and no hands-on technical actions are performed
The lowest-cost, lowest-disruption way to test an incident response plan, compared with a full simulation or live exercise
Tailgating: Following an authorized person through a secured door or checkpoint without separate credentials
Happens without the authorized person's consent or knowledge; piggybacking is with consent
Mitigations: access control vestibules (mantraps) and security guards
Technical control: Implemented with technology (hardware, software or firmware) to protect systems and data
Examples: firewalls, encryption, antivirus, ACLs, MFA, IDS/IPS
If a machine or code does the protecting, the category is technical
Pair with a type: a firewall is preventive, an IDS detective, automated restoration from backup corrective
Technical debt: Accumulated cost of shortcuts, quick fixes and outdated components in code or infrastructure
Must eventually be repaid through rework
In security it expands the attack surface and makes patching and automation harder
A drawback of automation: poorly maintained scripts and ad-hoc integrations become debt
Threat: Any circumstance, event or actor with the potential to cause harm to an asset by exploiting a vulnerability
Risk is a function of threat and vulnerability
In a scenario, tell the threat apart from the weakness it targets
Threat actor: Individual or group carrying out, or able to carry out, an attack against an organization's systems
Types: nation-state, hacktivist, organized crime, insider, script kiddie
The exam asks you to classify an actor from a scenario
Threat hunting: Proactive search by analysts through networks and systems for threats that evaded automated tools
Does not wait for an alert
Hypothesis-driven, often with an assume-breach mindset
Starts from threat intelligence and indicators of compromise
Threat intelligence: Evidence-based knowledge about existing or emerging threats
Covers actor tactics, techniques, indicators and motivations
Sources: open-source intelligence, closed or commercial feeds, information-sharing organizations such as ISACs
Drives threat hunting and IoC detection
Threat scope reduction: Limits the number of resources, paths and privileges any single subject can reach
Shrinks the blast radius if that subject is compromised
The reason for microsegmentation and least privilege
Three-way handshake: Three messages that set up a TCP connection before any data is sent: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK
SYN flood: many SYN packets and the handshake is never completed, exhausting the server's resources
Defenses: SYN cookies, rate limiting, shorter timeouts, a firewall or IPS in front of the server
Time-of-day restrictions: Permit logins or resource use only during defined hours or days, such as business hours
A rule-based control that reduces exposure to off-hours attacks
May conflict with on-call staff, so manage exceptions
Tokenization: Replaces sensitive data, such as a credit card number, with a non-sensitive placeholder token
The original is stored securely in a separate token vault
The token has no mathematical relationship to the original, so it cannot be reversed without the vault
Different from encryption and hashing; common in PCI DSS scenarios
Trade secret: Confidential business information that gives a competitive advantage because it is kept secret
Examples: a formula, process or customer list
No registration, and protection lasts only while it stays secret, unlike patents (public and time-limited)
A leak can destroy the protection, so NDAs, least privilege and DLP matter
Trojan horse: Malware disguised as legitimate or desirable software that tricks users into installing it
Often delivers a hidden malicious payload
A common vector for backdoors and spyware
Trunk port: Switch port that carries traffic for multiple VLANs at once, adding an 802.1Q tag to each frame
Used between switches or toward a router or firewall
An access port carries a single VLAN without a tag
VLAN hopping tries switch spoofing or double tagging against the native VLAN
Defenses: set user ports to access, disable trunk negotiation (DTP), move the native VLAN off VLAN 1, prune VLANs
Typosquatting: Registering a domain that is a common misspelling or slight variation of a legitimate one
Catches users who mistype the URL and lures them to a malicious site
Example: a single swapped or doubled letter
Delivers malware or harvests credentials; brand impersonation can happen without a lookalike domain
Unknown environment: Black box penetration test: the tester starts with no prior information
Must perform reconnaissance like an external attacker
The most realistic but slowest and most expensive
Findings reflect what an outsider could discover
Unskilled attacker: Low-skill attacker, often called a script kiddie
Relies on pre-made tools, scripts and exploits written by others
Motivated by curiosity, bragging rights or chaos, not a sophisticated goal
Lowest sophistication and resources; noisy and easy to detect, but can still do damage, so patch against known exploits
Vendor assessment: Evaluating a supplier's security posture and risk before and during the relationship
Methods: questionnaires, pen test results, internal audit evidence, independent assessments, supply chain analysis, right to audit
Alongside vendor selection (due diligence, conflict of interest), agreements and ongoing monitoring
Version control: System that tracks and stores every change to files such as source code, configurations and documentation
Records who changed what and when, so changes can be compared, audited and rolled back
Supports change management, secure development (Git) and recovery from bad changes
Protect repositories from leaked credentials and unauthorized commits; require reviews
Video surveillance: Cameras, often recording continuously, that monitor and capture activity in and around a facility
Used for deterrence, detection and post-incident investigation
Primarily a detective control and deterrent, not preventive
Footage supports investigations and chain of custody for physical evidence
Virtualization: Uses a hypervisor to run multiple virtual machines on one piece of physical hardware
Each VM has its own virtual hardware, operating system and applications
Risks: VM escape (breaking out of a guest to reach the hypervisor or host) and VM sprawl
Virus: Malicious code that attaches itself to a legitimate host file or program
Needs user action, such as opening the file, to run and spread
Unlike self-spreading worms, it requires a host file and human interaction
Variants include macro viruses and polymorphic viruses
Vishing: Social engineering attack over voice calls, including VoIP
Tricks victims into revealing sensitive information or taking harmful actions
The voice or phone-call variant of phishing
Often combined with caller ID spoofing
VLAN hopping: Lets an attacker send traffic into a VLAN they should not reach
Switch spoofing: tricking a port into trunk mode
Double tagging: stacking tags so the native VLAN passes the frame on
Mitigations: disable unused ports and DTP auto-negotiation, set access ports explicitly, keep user traffic off VLAN 1 and the native VLAN
VM escape: Code inside a virtual machine breaks out of its isolation
Interacts with the hypervisor or other VMs on the same host
Rare but severe: one compromised VM can expose the host and its neighbors
Mitigate by patching the hypervisor, minimizing host features, segmenting workloads, monitoring
VM sprawl: Uncontrolled growth of virtual machines that are easy to create but never tracked, patched or retired
Leaves unmanaged systems that expand the attack surface
Prevent with lifecycle management, ownership and tagging, regular audits and automated decommissioning
Vulnerability: Weakness in a system, process or control that a threat could exploit to cause harm
The weakness itself, distinct from the threat (the danger) and the exploit (the method)
Vulnerability scanning: Automated process that examines systems, networks and applications for known weaknesses
Compares them with a database of known vulnerabilities, such as missing patches or misconfigurations
Produces a report ranked by severity
Non-intrusive and automated, unlike penetration testing, which actively exploits findings
The discovery phase before remediation or deeper testing
War driving: Driving or walking around with a laptop or phone to find and map wireless networks
Often noting which are open or weakly secured
War chalking marks discoveries with symbols
Reconnaissance for wireless attacks; mitigate with WPA3, disabling WPS and limiting signal leakage outside the building
Warm site: Recovery site with hardware, power and network connectivity in place
No current data or fully configured systems
Data and applications must be restored from backups first, which takes hours to days
A middle ground on cost and recovery time between hot and cold; RPO depends on the backup schedule
Watering hole attack: Threat actor compromises a website frequently visited by a specific target group
Targets a trusted third-party site rather than the victim directly
Often used by advanced persistent threats against specific industries
Web filter: Blocks or allows web access by URL, domain, content category, reputation or keywords
Implemented as an endpoint agent, a centralized proxy or a cloud service
Methods: agent-based versus centralized proxy, URL scanning, content categorization, block rules, reputation
Also blocks known malware and phishing sites
Whaling: Spear phishing that targets high-profile individuals such as executives or senior leadership
Often involves fraudulent wire transfer requests: business email compromise or CEO fraud
Recognize it by the senior-executive target
Wildcard certificate: Single certificate using an asterisk in its common name, such as *.example.com
Secures an unlimited number of subdomains under one domain
Simplifies management and cuts cost across many subdomains
Trade-off: if the private key is compromised, every covered subdomain is at risk at once
Wireless jamming: Denial-of-service attack that transmits radio noise on the same frequency as a wireless network
Detect with spectrum analysis; mitigate by locating and removing the source, changing channels, or using wired links for critical systems
Worm: Self-replicating malware that spreads independently across networks
Needs no host file and no user interaction
Unlike a virus, which needs a host file and often user action
Classic example: exploiting a network service vulnerability
Zero trust: Security model that assumes no user, device or network segment is inherently trusted
Requires continuous verification for every access request, regardless of location
Zero-day: Vulnerability unknown to the vendor or public, with no available patch
Exploitable until it is discovered and fixed
The most dangerous vulnerability type: no signature or patch exists yet
Often paired with advanced persistent threat scenarios
